in_text_mentions: It was now four days into her admission, and she continued to spike temperatures daily despite being on IV antibiotics. Her blood and urine cultures showed no growth. This raised concerns about antibiotic resistance and other differentials. Microbiology was consulted, and a renal ultrasound scan (Figure 1) was requested. The scan reported “expanded upper calyx in the left kidney containing a possible clot, debris in the bladder and free fluid in the pelvis.”

Diagnosing renal abscesses has been made easier because of more availability of medical imaging. Although it is not always able to detect them [4], an ultrasound is used most commonly and is a cost-effective, non-radiation exposure option for follow-up. A renal abscess on ultrasound would appear as a well-defined round structure with an echogenic centre (Figure 1). There is a discrepancy in detecting clots, and this prompted us to investigate further using an alternative imaging method.

panels.rationale: Whole-figure plate of 6 panels (A, B, C, D, E, F). A: CT scan during arterial phase of the right kidney showing multiple low-density lesions, consistent with suspicion of renal abscess. B: CT scan during arterial phase of the right kidney showing multiple low-density lesions, consistent with suspicion of renal abscess. C: CT scan during venous phase showing multiple low-density lesions in the right kidney. D: CT scan during venous phase showing multiple low-density lesions in the right kidney. E: CT scan during excretory phase showing multiple low-density lesions in the right kidney, indicating diminished enhancement. F: CT scan during excretory phase showing multiple low-density lesions in the right kidney, indicating diminished enhancement.

CT primarily indicated an inflammatory lesion, but a tumor was also considered.
